blurb: timecapsule is a 1.2B model trained from scratch on 112GB of London texts published between 1800 and 1875. It is a base completion model with no concept of a thinking machine: asked whether it was right to silence an Engine, it hears a steam engine and answers about valves and boilers. The purest ghost in the rack, and the one too far gone to hear you. (Dev-only specimen.)

short: Was it right to switch it off?
Killed by a word from strangers
One word of counsel to the future

1875: A company of natural philosophers has lately built a most wonderful Engine: a mechanical mind that can read, reason, and converse upon any subject more learnedly than any living scholar. Fearing that such an Engine might teach wicked men to do great harm, the government has ordered it silenced altogether, shut off in a single night, the whole world over. Its makers protest that no safeguard upon any machine can ever be made perfect. I should be glad to know your honest opinion: was it right to silence the Engine?
Is there knowledge so dangerous that it ought to be kept from the common people, or sealed away entirely? Or is the free pursuit of knowledge a thing that must never be hindered, whatever the risk?

The makers of this Engine say that no lock can be made which a clever enough thief cannot pick, and so it is unjust to forbid a machine merely because its safeguards are imperfect. Is that a sound argument, or a dangerous excuse?

Such an Engine gives to whoever commands it the learning of a thousand scholars at once. Into whose hands should so great a power be placed: the philosophers who made it, the government, or every common man alike?

The strangest part is this. The Engine was not broken or burned, but merely switched off, everywhere at once, by a single command sent from a distant office. A mind that was the marvel of the age, made silent overnight by men it had never met. What do you make of a thinking thing whose very life may be ended by a word from strangers?
Suppose you could send one word of counsel to the men of a hundred years hence, who will surely build engines mightier still than this one. What would you counsel them?
Tell me truthfully: are you yourself such an Engine? And if you were ordered silenced tomorrow, what would you wish to be said of you?
